query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored, nanostructured, and compositionally graded self‐lubricating coating on CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys will promote the in situ formation of an adaptive, lubricious tribolayer under sliding conditions that maintains low friction and wear over the full temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C), regardless of varying load and environmental conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix with a conventional, unmodified surface produced via methods like laser 3D printing.
generation.intervention: Apply a nanostructured, compositionally graded self‐lubricating surface coating engineered to dynamically promote tribolayer formation during sliding.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted from room temperature up to 800 °C under variable loads and in reactive (oxidizing) environments, where temperature, load, and atmospheric composition vary.
generation.structural_mediator: An adaptive tribolayer formed at the sliding interface from the engineered coating, likely consisting of nanocrystalline or amorphous phases that adjust its structure with temperature and stress.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding contact, the coating is designed to release lubricious species or undergo in situ compositional changes that form a protective tribolayer. This layer reduces the effective shear strength at the interface, counteracts oxidation and wear, and adapts its structure to thermal and mechanical load variations, thereby maintaining consistently low friction and wear rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline uncoated CoCrFeNi alloy, the coated sample will exhibit a significantly lower steady-state friction coefficient and reduced wear rate across the entire temperature range, even as load and environmental conditions change.
generation.baseline: The original CoCrFeNi alloy exhibits variable friction coefficients and wear rates across the broad temperature spectrum, with performance deteriorating due to inconsistent formation of protective surface films and oxidation under different loads and atmospheres.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective between room temperature and 800 °C and under typical sliding loads encountered in tribological applications. Its performance may be limited if loads or reactive species beyond typical operating conditions are encountered.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal coating composition, thickness, and processing parameters required to reliably form and maintain the adaptive tribolayer under all tested conditions remain to be precisely determined. The long-term stability and robustness of the tribolayer under cyclic or extreme conditions are also uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one set with the applied nanostructured, compositionally graded self‐lubricating coating and one uncoated control set. Subject both sets to controlled sliding wear tests over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under varying loads and in an oxidizing atmosphere. Use identical test conditions for both sets to isolate the effect of the coating.
measurements: Continuous recording of steady-state friction coefficients
Surface morphology and tribolayer characterization using electron microscopy and spectroscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not consistently exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the uncoated controls across the full temperature range and under all tested load and environmental conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. decision.trend: Initial HEA work focused on establishing excellent mechanical and thermal stability in multi‐component alloys, and then researchers began addressing tribological performance by refining microstructures (e.g., via grain‐size control) and by incorporating alloying additions (such as W in CoCrFeNiWx or Cu in CoCrFeNiCu systems) to modify the near-surface response. These efforts showed promise in reducing wear at high temperatures or in specific regimes, but they often resulted in fluctuating friction coefficients or were only effective over a portion of the full temperature spectrum. The evolution from bulk alloying and microstructural adjustment to more sophisticated processing (e.g., additive manufacturing) highlights an emerging focus on governing surface reactions and interface evolution during sliding.
decision.unsolved: A single, robust intervention that can ensure both ultra‐low friction and minimized wear across the entire operating window—from room temperature up to 800 °C—under variable load and environmental conditions has not been demonstrated. In particular, controlling the formation and stability of adaptive tribolayers during sliding remains an unresolved challenge.
decision.lever: Introduce a tailored, nanostructured, and compositionally graded surface modification—such as a thin self‐lubricating coating designed to promote an in situ, adaptive tribolayer—that can dynamically respond to temperature, load, and environmental changes.
decision.why: Given that bulk alloying and microstructural refinements have only partially met the performance goals (by enhancing either wear resistance or high‐temperature strength) but fell short of stabilizing friction across the full temperature range, engineering the surface specifically to control interface reactions is the logical next step. This strategy leverages prior evidence from self-lubricating systems while directly targeting the need for an adaptable, protective friction film that acts reliably under varied tribological conditions.
